title: DIAL: Direction-Informed Adaptive Learning for LLM Agents
claim: A signal assumed to predict compute benefit in a fixed direction actually reverses sign across settings, undermining fixed-direction gating.
layout: Single horizontal diverging bar chart, top-to-bottom, shaded region marking prior assumption
description: A single horizontal bar chart shows Spearman correlation between token entropy and utility for six environments: APPS, WebShop, Plancraft, FEVER, TWExpress and HotpotQA. The x-axis runs from -0.4 to 0.4, with a dashed vertical line at zero. The right half (rho > 0) is shaded light pink and titled in bold red 'prior-work assumption: rho > 0'. APPS (+0.32) and WebShop (+0.13) have red bars extending right into the shaded region. Plancraft (-0.02) has a tiny gray bar near zero. FEVER (-0.12), TWExpress (-0.29) and HotpotQA (-0.33) have blue bars extending left, outside the assumed region. Value labels sit at the bar ends. The eye goes first to the red title and the red-versus-blue split around zero.
caption: The fixed-direction assumption fails on half of the environments. Spearman correlation $\rho(entropy, U)$ across six environments on Qwen3-4B.
abstract: Adaptive test-time compute for LLM agents aims to invoke extra computation only when it improves performance. Existing methods typically use confidence-, uncertainty-, or difficulty-based gates, assuming a fixed direction from the gating signal through compute need to the value of computation. This makes gating a utility-calibration problem: gating signals should align with whether extra computation improves the final outcome over the base policy. We show that this alignment is unstable: the same signal predicts rollout benefit in one setting and rollout harm in another, with reversals across environments and backbones even when the task is fixed. Wrong-direction gates can therefore worsen performance by precisely selecting harmful states. This reversal reflects a deeper distinction between compute need and compute suitability: a high uncertainty signal may indicate decision-difficult states where rollouts help compare alternatives, or intervention-unsuitable states where the current context does not support useful rollout-based improvement. Under this two-source model, fixed-direction gates are unreliable across heterogeneous settings. To address this, we propose DIAL ( D irection- I nformed A daptive L earning), a sparse gate trained from signal-agnostic counterfactual exploration to learn the utility direction of state features per (environment, backbone). Across six environments and three backbones, DIAL yields a stronger overall success-cost trade-off than fixed-direction baselines. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/zmli6/DIAL.
